concepts.title: Meaning, Features and Importance of Directing
concepts.definition: The managerial function that steers people at work through instructions, guidance, counselling, motivation and leadership so that the organisation's objectives are actually pursued; it is the spark that puts plans to work and runs at every level for as long as the organisation lives.
concepts.key_idea: Four marks: it initiates action, exists wherever superior-subordinate relations exist, never stops, and flows down the hierarchy; its worth lies in starting action, joining individual efforts, drawing out potential, easing change and keeping the organisation balanced.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 84-254 (Meaning; characteristics i-iv; importance i-v)
question_patterns: what is meant by directing as a function of management
state the characteristics of directing
why does directing flow from top to bottom and never stop at any level
why is directing called a continuous process at every level of management
explain the importance of directing for an organisation
how does directing help in introducing changes smoothly
which function of management initiates action in an organisation

solution_steps.explain: Directing covers instructing, guiding, counselling, motivating and leading employees toward the objectives.
It initiates action, occurs at every level, continues throughout the organisation's life, and moves from top to bottom.
It starts effort toward goals, integrates individual contributions, develops potential, lowers resistance to change, and brings stability.

concepts.title: Principles of Directing
concepts.definition: Eight guides for effective direction: draw the maximum contribution from each person, harmonise individual and organisational aims, keep one boss per person, pick techniques that fit the subordinate, communicate clearly with feedback, use informal groups wisely, lead well, and always follow up on orders given.
concepts.key_idea: Match the principle to the case -- rewards suiting each worker show appropriateness of technique; a manager reviewing orders shows follow through.
question_patterns: explain any three principles of directing
which principle of directing insists on one boss for one person
what does the principle of harmony of objectives require
why should direction techniques suit the needs of subordinates
what is meant by follow through in directing
how does maximum individual contribution guide a manager

solution_steps.explain: Recall the eight principles of directing and select the one the case or statement refers to.
For instance, unity of command here means instructions reach a person from one superior only, avoiding confusion.
Money motivates some workers, promotion others -- so techniques must be chosen to fit the person.

concepts.title: Supervision as an Element of Directing
concepts.definition: The overseeing of subordinates' work with guidance and instruction so that resources are used well and targets are met; it is both an element every manager performs and the job title of the operative-level manager standing directly above the workers.
concepts.key_idea: The supervisor is the workers' guide, friend and philosopher and the link carrying management's ideas down and workers' problems up.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 400-537 (Supervision, two meanings; importance i-vii)
question_patterns: what is meant by supervision in directing
why is the supervisor called a link between workers and management
state the importance of supervision in an organisation
how does a supervisor maintain group unity among workers
in what sense is a supervisor a guide friend and philosopher to workers

solution_steps.action: Give the two senses of supervision
solution_steps.explain: As an element of directing it means overseeing and guiding effort; as a position it means the lowest managerial rank above workers.
Day-to-day contact, link between workers and management, group unity, meeting targets, on-the-job training, morale, feedback.

solution_steps.action: Note why the role is vital
solution_steps.explain: No other manager touches the workers directly, so quality, discipline and grievances all pass through the supervisor.

concepts.title: Motivation -- Concept, Features and Process
concepts.definition: The process of stirring subordinates to act in the desired way so that organisational goals are served; it begins with an inner state called a motive, works through stimulation called motivation, and applies tools called motivators such as pay, praise or promotion.
concepts.key_idea: It is an internal feeling producing goal-directed behaviour, may be positive or negative, and affects different people differently; the chain runs from unsatisfied need to tension, drives, search behaviour, satisfaction and relief of tension.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 538-707 (motive, motivation, motivators; features i-iv; motivation process and Ramu example)
question_patterns: what is meant by motivation
distinguish between motive motivation and motivator
explain the process of motivation with the help of a diagram
state the features of motivation
how does an unsatisfied need generate behaviour explain the motivation cycle
can motivation be negative give examples

solution_steps.explain: Motive: the inner state that moves behaviour. Motivation: the process of stimulating action toward goals. Motivator: the technique used, like bonus or recognition.
Internal feeling, goal-directed behaviour, positive or negative forms, complex and uneven across people.
Unsatisfied need creates tension, tension drives search behaviour, satisfying the need ends the tension -- as hunger drove Ramu to search for food.

concepts.title: Maslow's Need Hierarchy Theory
concepts.definition: Abraham Maslow's ladder of five human needs, rising from basic physiological needs such as food and shelter, through safety, belonging and esteem, to self-actualisation, the drive to become all one is capable of becoming.
concepts.key_idea: Assumptions to cite: behaviour flows from needs, needs stand in a hierarchy, a satisfied need no longer motivates, and the next level pulls only after the lower one is met -- basic salary serves the bottom rung, pension plans the second, friendship the third, status the fourth, growth the top.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 828-940 (Maslow's theory: five needs i-v, assumptions i-iv, criticism)
question_patterns: discuss maslow's need hierarchy theory of motivation
name the five levels of needs in maslow's hierarchy with examples
which level of maslow's hierarchy does job security belong to
state the assumptions on which maslow's theory rests
why can a satisfied need no longer motivate a person
which organisational incentives satisfy the esteem needs of employees

solution_steps.explain: Physiological, safety and security, affiliation and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation -- from bottom to top.
Hunger maps to basic salary; stability of income to pension plans; friendship to cordial colleagues; status to job title; growth to achievement of goals.
Needs drive behaviour; they follow a hierarchy; a met need stops motivating; the next level attracts only after the lower is satisfied.
Identify the employee's current need level before choosing the incentive.

concepts.title: Financial Incentives
concepts.definition: Motivators payable in money or measurable in money: pay and allowances, productivity-linked wages, bonus, a share in profits, stock options that make employees co-owners, retirement benefits such as provident fund and pension, and perquisites like housing, car allowance or medical aid.
concepts.key_idea: Money buys daily needs plus social standing, so it stays the most direct incentive; stock options go further by creating a feeling of ownership.
question_patterns: explain any four financial incentives used to motivate employees
which incentive gives employees shares at a price below the market rate
how does profit sharing motivate workers
name the retirement benefits that act as financial incentives
a firm grants car allowance and housing to managers name the incentive
what is meant by productivity linked wage incentives

solution_steps.explain: Financial incentives are direct monetary rewards or benefits measurable in money.
Pay and allowances, productivity-linked wages, bonus, profit sharing, co-partnership and stock options, retirement benefits, perquisites.
For example, stock options allot shares below market price, breeding ownership feelings and loyalty.

concepts.title: Non-Financial Incentives
concepts.definition: Motivators aimed at psychological, social and emotional needs rather than the purse: status, a supportive organisational climate, career advancement opportunities, enriched jobs with autonomy and challenge, recognition programmes, job security, employee participation in decisions, and empowerment with greater autonomy.
concepts.key_idea: Money alone cannot satisfy every need; a promotion may raise pay but its real pull is elevation, status and authority -- the psychological over the monetary.
question_patterns: explain any four non financial incentives for employees
free medical aid and education for employees children which incentive is highlighted
how does job enrichment act as a motivator
what is meant by employee empowerment and participation
which incentives satisfy the esteem needs of workers
why is status called a non financial incentive

solution_steps.explain: These incentives target psychological and social needs, sometimes touching money but never resting on it.
Status, organisational climate, career advancement, job enrichment, recognition, job security, participation, empowerment.
Medical aid and education for employees' children fall under perquisites within financial incentives -- but recognition or status cases belong here; classify with care.
Each instrument feeds esteem, belonging or growth needs that wages alone cannot reach.

concepts.title: Leadership -- Meaning, Features and Importance
concepts.definition: The art of influencing people so that they strive willingly toward group goals; it rests on the ability to build good interpersonal relations with followers and to draw their best contribution without coercion.
concepts.key_idea: Its features: the power to influence, a change agent for behaviour, interpersonal between leader and followers, aimed at common goals, and continuous; its worth shows in positive contribution, need fulfilment, smoother change, conflict handling and successor building -- and followers, by accepting leadership, co-create the leader.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 1252-1387 (definitions box; features i-v; importance i-v)
question_patterns: what is meant by leadership
state the features of leadership
why is leadership important for the success of an organisation
how does a leader help in introducing changes
leaders indicate the ability to influence others explain
how do followers make a person a good leader

solution_steps.explain: It is influencing people to strive voluntarily for organisational objectives.
Influence, behavioural change, interpersonal relations, common goals, continuous process.
Positive contribution of energies, personal support to followers, acceptance of change, conflict resolution, training of successors.

concepts.title: Leadership Styles
concepts.definition: Three patterns of using authority: the autocratic leader commands and expects obedience with one-way communication, the democratic leader consults subordinates before deciding, and the laissez-faire leader leaves followers free to set their own objectives, stepping in only to support and supply information.
concepts.key_idea: Autocracy buys speed and discipline on the shop floor; democracy buys commitment through participation; free-rein buys creativity from capable teams -- a leader may blend styles as the situation demands.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 1388-1487 (Autocratic, Democratic, Laissez faire styles)
question_patterns: explain the different styles of leadership
which style of leadership does not believe in use of power unless absolutely essential
a manager who never likes to be contradicted which style does he follow
compare autocratic and democratic leadership styles
which leadership style suits a team of experts working on their own
what are the merits of participative leadership

solution_steps.action: Classify the leader from the case
solution_steps.explain: Orders and obedience point to autocratic; consultation to democratic; full freedom to laissez-faire.
One line on how authority and communication flow under it.
For instance, autocratic style speeds decisions but breeds stress and suppresses initiative.

concepts.title: Communication Process and Its Elements
concepts.definition: The exchange of ideas, facts and feelings between people so that a common understanding emerges; the chain runs from sender through encoding, media of transmission and decoding to receiver, with feedback closing the loop and noise threatening every link.
concepts.key_idea: Encoding turns ideas into words or gestures, decoding reverses the process at the receiver; noise is any obstruction -- bad phone lines, ambiguous symbols, an inattentive listener, prejudices, mismatched body language.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 1488-1601 (definitions; elements of communication process i-viii; noise examples)
question_patterns: explain the elements of the communication process
which element involves converting the message into words symbols and gestures
what is meant by noise in communication with examples
what role does feedback play in communication
draw and explain the communication process diagram
distinguish between encoding and decoding in communication

solution_steps.explain: It is the two-way process of sharing information until sender and receiver reach common understanding.
Sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback -- with noise able to strike any stage.
Obstructions range from faulty encoding and poor phone lines to inattention, prejudices and distorting gestures.

concepts.title: Importance of Communication
concepts.definition: The reasons the function is central to managing: it underpins coordination, keeps the enterprise working smoothly, supplies the information behind decisions, raises managerial efficiency, builds cooperation and industrial peace, grounds leadership, and lifts morale and motivation.
concepts.key_idea: A manager spends most of the working day communicating; when communication stops, organised activity itself ceases.
question_patterns: explain the importance of communication in management
how does communication act as the basis of coordination
why is communication called the basis of decision making
how does communication boost the morale of employees
what happens to an enterprise when communication stops

solution_steps.explain: Coordination, smooth working, decision making, managerial efficiency, cooperation and peace, leadership, morale and motivation.
For decisions, relevant information must travel to the manager; without it no meaningful choice can be made.
Communication oils the whole management process and keeps the organisation at work.

concepts.title: Formal and Informal Communication
concepts.definition: Official messages move through the channels drawn on the organisation chart -- vertical, upward or downward, and horizontal between sister divisions -- over networks like the single chain, wheel, circular, free flow and inverted V; unofficial exchange, the grapevine, ignores these lines entirely and spreads in single strand, gossip, probability or cluster patterns.
concepts.key_idea: Grapevine talk travels fast, distorts easily and hides its source, yet a wise manager taps it to sound out reactions -- the cluster network is the most common.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 1726-1907 (Formal and informal communication; networks; grapevine networks)
question_patterns: what is informal communication
state the different networks of grapevine communication
which grapevine network is most popular in organisations
distinguish between formal and informal communication
a leave application moving up to the boss is which type of communication
explain the wheel and circular networks of formal communication

solution_steps.explain: Recorded messages on official channels are formal; canteen chatter and transfer rumours are informal grapevine.
Formal: single chain, wheel, circular, free flow, inverted V. Grapevine: single strand, gossip, probability, cluster.
It gives speed and honest reactions but breeds distortion and rumour; manage it, do not abolish it.

concepts.title: Barriers to Communication and Their Remedies
concepts.definition: Four families of obstruction: semantic barriers of badly expressed or wrongly translated words, technical jargon and ambiguous symbols; psychological barriers like premature evaluation, inattention, loss in transmission and distrust; organisational barriers from rigid rules, status distance and layered structures; and personal barriers such as fear of challenge or unwillingness to speak up.
concepts.key_idea: Remedies mirror the barriers -- clarify ideas first, suit the receiver's level, consult before sending, watch language and tone, convey useful content, ensure feedback, think of the future, follow up, and listen well.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs107.txt lines 1893-2375 (Barriers: semantic, psychological, organisational, personal; improving communication effectiveness i-ix)
question_patterns: what are the common barriers to effective communication
explain the semantic barriers to communication
a boss instructs take care of our guest and misunderstandings follow which barrier is this
suggest measures to overcome the barriers to communication
which psychological barrier operates when a receiver judges the message before it ends
how does status of superiors obstruct communication in an organisation

solution_steps.action: Sort the barrier into its family
solution_steps.explain: Meaning troubles are semantic, state-of-mind troubles psychological, structure troubles organisational, and individual habits personal.
For example, unclarified assumptions leave the receiver guessing what take care of our guest really covers.
Clarify ideas before sending, match the receiver's understanding level, seek feedback, and follow up on instructions.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A reputed hostel provides medical aid and free education to the children of its employees. Name the incentive, its category, and two more incentives of the same category.

solution_template.explain: This is a perquisite -- a fringe benefit over and above salary.
Perquisites belong to the financial incentives category, being benefits measurable in money.

solution_template.action: Give two more of the same kind
solution_template.explain: Pay and allowances, and retirement benefits such as provident fund or pension, sit in the same financial category.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A departmental manager is inflexible: once he decides, he refuses contradiction, so staff feel stressed, take little initiative and fear speaking up. Which leadership style is he using and what should change?

solution_template.explain: Orders without contradiction mark the autocratic or authoritarian style.
One-way communication breeds stress, suppresses initiative and silences opinions -- exactly the case symptoms.
A democratic style that consults subordinates would lift participation, initiative and morale.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Workers always plead inability when new work arrives and the supervisor cannot cope with rising demand. Which element of directing can help him handle the problem?

solution_template.explain: Unwillingness despite ability is a motivation problem, not a skill problem.
Motivation -- stimulating people to act willingly toward the goals.
Suitable financial and non-financial incentives, plus praise and recognition, can turn reluctance into willing effort.
